name: jemalloc
baseline: phkmalloc (FreeBSD libc malloc, the incumbent jemalloc replaced)
workload: malloc-test microbenchmark (Lever & Boreham 2000): tight alloc/dealloc loop, 40,000,000 cycles total divided across up to 20 threads, one 512-byte object per cycle; plus five single-threaded real programs (cca, cfrac, GhostScript, sh6bench, smlng) and a MySQL super-smack query-throughput benchmark
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded programs (mean run time, phkmalloc vs jemalloc, from the paper's tables): cca 77.73s vs 69.37s (~1.12x, derived from page data); gs 42.48s vs 34.24s (~1.24x, derived from page data); sh6bench 6.96s vs 4.50s (~1.55x, derived from page data); smlng 13.89s vs 11.49s (~1.21x, derived from page data); cfrac 11.45s vs 10.55s (~1.09x, derived from page data). Multi-threaded malloc-test (Figure 6, log scale): jemalloc plateaus at roughly 3x10^7 allocations/sec from 4 threads upward (with a dip above 16 threads), while phkmalloc falls below 1x10^5 allocations/sec by 10 threads and was not run beyond 10 threads (on the order of 400x at 10 threads, derived from page data, approximate reading of the log-scale plot)
hardware: four-processor system (dual-dual AMD Opteron 275), FreeBSD-CURRENT/amd64, April 2006
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; default allocator for FreeBSD libc, used by Redis, historically Firefox, and many large-scale services at Meta
tradeoffs: multiple arenas reduce contention but can raise peak memory in low-concurrency cases; larger tuning surface (narenas, dirty/muzzy decay_ms, percpu_arena); jemalloc's own README/TUNING.md carries no numeric benchmarks
caveats: Evidence is jemalloc's own founding paper (Evans, 'A Scalable Concurrent malloc(3) Implementation for FreeBSD', BSDCan 2006), which compares against phkmalloc (FreeBSD's libc malloc at the time) and dlmalloc 2.8.3, not glibc. BSDCan is a practitioner conference, not a peer-reviewed venue, and benchmarks are 'available upon request' with no compiler/flags, so tier C. Numbers are ~20 years old on a dual-dual Opteron 275. dlmalloc beat jemalloc on cfrac, gs and sh6bench. On MySQL super-smack the paper says phkmalloc's median throughput is 'typically about the same as for jemalloc'; jemalloc's gain there is in worst-case variability. No modern jemalloc-vs-glibc numbers were found in the repo (README, TUNING.md have none).

name: snmalloc
workload: ISMM 2019 paper micro-benchmarks: a symmetric workload (each thread allocates, swaps with another thread, and deallocates) and a producer/consumer workload (malloc-test, half the threads allocate batches of 4096 objects sized 8-2048B, the other half deallocate), swept from 1 to 64 threads; also a SPECspeed 2017 Integer suite run and two real-application integrations (FaRM, FreeBSD libc)
claimed_speedup: Figure 5 (producer/consumer malloc-test, random 8-2048B objects, thread sweep): at 64 threads snmalloc ~190M and snmalloc-1mib ~220M allocs/sec vs glibc ~47M (~4x, derived from page data, approximate chart reading). Figure 4 (symmetric workload): at 64 threads snmalloc ~180M vs glibc ~105M allocs/sec (~1.7x, derived from page data, approximate), with tcmalloc/jemalloc/SuperMalloc ahead of snmalloc. Figure 6 (producer/consumer by object size): snmalloc ~570M vs glibc ~110M at 16B (~5x) and ~250M vs ~27M at 1KiB (~9x), with glibc near zero above ~4KiB while snmalloc stays at or above ~120M up to 32KiB (derived from page data, approximate). SPECspeed Integer (Fig 12), verbatim: snmalloc performs "as well or better than the widely used jemalloc, tcmalloc and glibc's allocator on all benchmarks".
hardware: Micro-benchmarks (Figs 4-10): Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard F64s_v2 VM, 64 vCPUs on dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8168, 128 GB RAM; SPECspeed suite: Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard D3_v2 VM, 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon E5-2673), 14 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars; Rust bindings via the snmalloc-rs crate (linked from README)
tradeoffs: message-passing remote deallocation adds an outgoing-buffer/batching mechanism (tunable, default 1MiB) which trades a little memory for throughput; higher implementation complexity than simple thread-caching allocators; paper notes SuperMalloc needed >100s to reach peak throughput while snmalloc/glibc/rpmalloc warm up in about 20s
caveats: Speedups vs glibc are read off linear-scale throughput charts (Figs 4-6), not stated as ratios in prose, so they are approximate. The only verbatim vs-glibc statement is the SPECspeed 'as well or better' sentence. On the symmetric workload (Fig 4), jemalloc and tcmalloc beat snmalloc. No compiler or flags are given, so B not A. The FreeBSD 12.0 libc integration in the paper was the authors' own experiment (24 Makefile lines) to show ease of adoption; it did not make snmalloc FreeBSD's default malloc, and FreeBSD libc still ships jemalloc. The README says the implementation 'has evolved significantly since the initial paper... most of the meta-data layout has changed', so current performance may differ from the 2019 figures.

name: TCMalloc (google/tcmalloc)
workload: No specific benchmark named; docs/overview.md frames TCMalloc as "an alternative to the one provided by the C standard library (on Linux usually through glibc)" and states it is "designed to be more efficient at scale than other implementations", without a stated test.
stars_or_usage: 5.4k stars; used throughout Google's production C++ services
tradeoffs: hard dependency on Abseil; default per-CPU caching fast path requires Linux RSEQ support (kernel >=4.18), else falls back to slower per-thread caching; heavier build/dependency footprint than gperftools' tcmalloc
caveats: No public numeric benchmark of google/tcmalloc vs glibc malloc, std::allocator, or operator new/delete was found in the repo's docs, so this is tier D on the qualitative overview.md claim. Peer-reviewed numeric evidence exists only against TCMalloc's OWN legacy pageheap: Hunter, Kennelly et al., 'Beyond malloc efficiency to fleet efficiency: a hugepage-aware memory allocator' (OSDI 2021). TEMERAIRE improved RPS by 7.7% and cut RAM by 2.4% across 8 applications (abstract). Table 1 averages +5.2% throughput across WSC apps. Fleet IPC rose 1.2%, and pageheap overhead fell from 14.3% to 10.6% (Fig. 15). Redis 6.0.9 gained +0.75% with periodic release off and +0.44% with it on (Intel Skylake Xeon, LLVM cd442157cf -O3, 2000 trials of redis-benchmark with 1,000,000 requests each). That is TCMalloc vs TCMalloc, not vs a listed baseline. google/tcmalloc is the documented successor ('abseil tcmalloc') to gperftools' tcmalloc, whose quoted glibc comparison is recorded under the 'gperftools TCMalloc' entry.

name: Eigen
workload: Single-threaded float and double BLAS operations (AXPY, DOT, GEMV, GEMM, TRSM, SYRK) and LAPACK operations (POTRF, GETRF, GEQRF, SYEV, GESDD, GEEV), measured over square and rectangular shapes. The Eigen arm uses no external BLAS. It is compared with OpenBLAS 0.3.26 (one thread, bundled LAPACK), Intel oneMKL 2025.3 (sequential) and BLIS 2.1 (BLAS only). Method: Google Benchmark 1.8.3, 10 repetitions of at least 0.2 s each, median GFLOP/s per cell, 874 operation-shape cells.
claimed_speedup: The page reports the geometric mean of Eigen/OpenBLAS rate ratios for square shapes in each size band (above 1 means Eigen is faster). Double-precision bands are n<=16 / 24-128 / 192-1024 / 1536-16384. Results: GEMM 1.11 / 0.85 / 1.07 / 0.94. GEMV 2.23 / 1.63 / 1.08 / 1.07. DOT 4.90 / 2.44 / 1.10 / 1.03. TRSM 1.48 / 3.60 / 2.19 / 1.23. POTRF 1.38 / 1.25 / 1.50 / 1.25. SYEV 1.36 / 1.77 / 2.33 / 1.79. Eigen is slower on GEEV (0.45 at 192-1024) and on GESDD (0.60 / 0.80 / 0.90 at 24-16384). Compared with oneMKL, Eigen wins mostly at small sizes. At large sizes it is often slower (double GEMM 0.93, SYEV 0.37, GEEV 0.41 at 192-1024). A companion Zen 5 page (WSL2) shows double GEMM against OpenBLAS at 1.28 / 0.95 / 1.30 / 1.21.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, C++17; Eigen upstream master ab4f7316d with no external BLAS and no OpenMP
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y, one socket, 16 cores / 32 threads, bare metal. Benchmark pinned to one logical CPU (single-threaded, AVX-512). Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Linux 6.17.0-35-generic. Performance governor; frequency not locked.
stars_or_usage: 1,190 GitLab stars (GitLab project created 2019-11-21); foundational dependency of ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, PCL, OpenCV, g2o, Blender, and many other numerical/robotics/vision projects
tradeoffs: Header-only template library, so heavy expression-template usage can increase compile times; built-in kernels favor small/fixed-size matrices (avoiding BLAS call overhead) while very large dense problems are the case where linking an external BLAS/LAPACK backend is recommended instead of relying solely on Eigen's own kernels.
caveats: The Eigen team published this benchmark on its own site, and the harness is still in an open (unmerged) merge request, !2903. Results are mixed. Against OpenBLAS, Eigen is faster at small and medium sizes for level-1/2 BLAS and for several LAPACK operations (TRSM, POTRF, SYEV). For large GEMM and SYRK it is roughly at parity or slightly slower, and it is slower on GEEV and on mid-size GESDD. Against Intel oneMKL, Eigen is generally slower at large sizes. All measurements are single-threaded with frequency not locked. The older eigen.tuxfamily.org Benchmark page (BTL harness, March 2011) is now marked as a historical record.

name: moodycamel::ConcurrentQueue

caveats: Benchmark was run and published by the paper's authors, several of whom (Intel, branchfree.org's Geoff Langdale) are Hyperscan's own developers, so despite NSDI peer review it is not fully independent. The real-world HTTP traffic trace ('obtained at a cloud service provider') is not public, so exact reproduction needs a substitute trace; no explicit public artifact/script repo for the Snort/ruleset harness was found, only library versions and hardware/compiler, so tier capped at B rather than A. Some ratios exceed 50x (e.g. 183.3x) but compiler/hardware/library versions are stated and it is not a debug/-O0 build, so the hard-rule auto-cap-to-C does not apply.

name: Highway (vqsort)
workload: bench_sort benchmark sorting arrays of built-in types (e.g. f32, uniform32 distribution) up to 1e6 keys with AVX-512 (AVX3), comparing LLVM libc++ std::sort against vqsort, reporting output throughput in MB/s of sorted key bytes.
claimed_speedup: About 10x faster than LLVM's std::sort for large arrays of built-in types (as of 2022-06-07). README example: AVX3, f32, uniform32, 1.00E+06 keys: std::sort 54 MB/s vs vqsort 1143 MB/s (~21x on that specific case, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Clang (tested with 13.0.1 and 15.0.6), Bazel `-c opt` optimized build
hardware: Xeon 6154 (Skylake-X), clocked at 3 GHz
stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars; used in Google projects and backed by a peer-reviewed paper (arXiv:2205.05982)
tradeoffs: Full speedup needs SIMD-capable hardware (AVX2/AVX3/NEON/SVE) with runtime dispatch; not a stable sort; speedup magnitude varies a lot by instruction set, key type, and distribution; small-array performance was a later optimization added after the original headline number.
caveats: The README itself notes pdqsort-class scalar algorithms are 'about twice as fast as LLVM's std::sort' (as of 2023-06), so the 10x figure is specifically vs plain std::sort, not vs the best scalar competitor. Independent analysis by Lukas Bergdoll (sort-research-rs) found a performance bug (entropy fetched from the OS on every call) that was fixed in PR #1334 after the original numbers were published; some published figures predate that fix.

verification.tier_reason: hwy/contrib/sort/README.md states the '~10x vs LLVM's std::sort' claim (2022-06-07) and shows std 54 MB/s vs vq 1143 MB/s (AVX3, f32 uniform32, 1e6 keys) on a Xeon 6154 at 3 GHz. It names Clang 13.0.1/15.0.6 and `bazelisk build -c opt`. The public benchmark code is hwy/contrib/sort/bench_sort.cc.

GitHub reports license NOASSERTION, but LICENSE is dual Apache-2.0/BSD-3-Clause, so the record is correct. 5,873 stars, last commit 2026-09-23.

name: pdqsort
workload: Median cycles per element (rdtsc, bench/bench.cpp) sorting a std::vector<int> of 10^6 elements under 8 distributions (shuffled, shuffled 16 values, all equal, ascending, descending, pipe organ, push front, push middle), compared to GCC libstdc++ std::sort and std::stable_sort.
claimed_speedup: Approximate, read from the README bar chart (sorting 10^6 ints, cycles per element, i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz) (derived from page data). Vs GCC std::sort, pdqsort is faster on all 8 distributions: shuffled ~113 vs ~220 (~1.9x), shuffled 16 values ~20 vs ~84 (~4x), descending ~7 vs ~34 (~5x), pipe organ ~118 vs ~266 (~2.2x), push front ~45 vs ~319 (~7x), and more than 10x on all equal, ascending and push middle (~3-4 vs ~38-179). Vs std::stable_sort it is faster on shuffled (~113 vs ~273, ~2.4x) and most patterns, but slower on pipe organ (~118 vs ~51) and about equal on push front (~45 vs ~45).

hardware: i5-4670k @ 3.4GHz (stated in the x-axis label of the README benchmark chart)
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; algorithm concepts adopted in Rust's sort_unstable and referenced widely in later stdlib sort redesigns
tradeoffs: Not stable (no stable variant provided); branchless fast path only applies to arithmetic types with default std::less/std::greater; falls back to heapsort on adversarial inputs.
caveats: Numbers appear only in a bar-chart image (i.imgur.com/1RnIGBO.png), so the values are approximate readings. The CPU is printed in the chart's axis label (bars.py writes its cpu argument into the xlabel). Not faster than std::stable_sort on pipe organ (~2.3x slower) and about equal on push front. Only 10^6 ints are charted. GCC version and run date are unstated, so the libstdc++ tested is old. No commits since 2021-03-14 (more than 3 years), so abandoned.

name: ska_sort
workload: Nanoseconds-per-item sorting of integers, floats, structs (128-1024 bytes), and strings via radix sort / American flag sort (ska_sort), compared against std::sort across increasing array sizes and skewed distributions.
claimed_speedup: Blog post: 'I wrote a sorting algorithm that's twice as fast as std::sort for many inputs'. On ints from std::geometric_distribution(0.001) it is 'many times faster than std::sort'. For small collections it is 'never slower than std::sort (because it uses std::sort when the collection is too small)', because it stops recursing below 128 elements. Per-type results appear only as ns/item chart images.
stars_or_usage: 248 stars
tradeoffs: Not a comparison sort; requires an extractable radix key (integers, bit-tricked floats, strings, tuples); not stable; needs O(n) auxiliary buffer memory; benefit shrinks for very large keys or non-radix-friendly types.
caveats: The repo ships only ska_sort.hpp and ska_sort_tests_and_benchmarks.cpp, with no README and no numbers. The claim lives in the author's 2016 blog post, which states no compiler, flags or CPU model (tier C). The post admits it degrades toward O(n log n) behavior on millions of long strings, and a reader comment reports it slower than std::sort on 1.2 billion uint64_t (unverified). The license (BSL-1.0) is stated only in the file headers; there is no LICENSE file and GitHub reports none. No commits since 2017-05-15.

name: vergesort
workload: Cycles per element (rdtsc, bench/bench.cpp) sorting a std::vector<int> of one million ints under 12 distributions (shuffled, shuffled 16 values, all equal, ascending, descending, pipe organ, push front, push middle, ascending/descending sawtooth, alternating, alternating 16 values). The random-access version is compared against std::sort, std::stable_sort, heapsort and pdqsort. A second chart compares the bidirectional version against std::list::sort, and fallbacks.md compares with/without-vergesort runs over std::sort and std::stable_sort (libstdc++ MinGW 6.1.0), timsort, spreadsort, pdqsort and ska_sort.
claimed_speedup: Approximate, read from the README random-access chart (10^6 ints, cycles per element) (derived from page data). Vergesort beats libstdc++ std::sort on every distribution shown: shuffled ~365 vs ~713 (~2x, via its pdqsort fallback), pipe organ ~22 vs ~885, push front ~15 vs ~858, ascending and descending sawtooth ~63 vs ~325 (~5x). It beats std::stable_sort on most patterns (sawtooth ~63 vs ~165-198) but is slower on 'Alternating' (~307 vs ~185). The author notes the sawtooth patterns are biased toward vergesort.
compiler_and_flags: MinGW g++ 6.1.0 -std=c++1z -O2 -march=native
stars_or_usage: 73 stars
tradeoffs: Not stable; best case relies on data containing sorted runs of size > n/log n; the bidirectional-iterator variant's worst case is O(n^2) since it falls back to a median-of-9 quicksort instead of pdqsort.
caveats: Numbers appear only as chart images (imgur), so the values are approximate readings. No CPU model is stated anywhere, which caps the tier at C. Built with the old MinGW GCC 6.1.0. The win over std::sort on random data comes from the pdqsort fallback. Slower than std::stable_sort on the 'Alternating' pattern. The bidirectional version is slower than std::list::sort on the sawtooth and alternating patterns.
